01.summary: Smith to the Queen, Chartres, 17 Jan 1562/3 (Forbes ii 287-289): someone should be sent to the Admiral, now chief on the other side, and Mr Middlemore would be fit; the Guisians will make no agreement with the Queen; the Constable suspects the Guise and fears the ruin of the Châtillons; if the Admiral holds out, necessity will force an accord; the Queen should act with speed while the Huguenot faction is at her devotion. The 13 cipher passages of f. 157 are read as Forbes prints them.
01.en:
⟨On the 14th a secretary came with letters⟩ from the Cardinal of Lorraine.

⟨I think it most necessary that⟩ someone be sent to stay with the Admiral (Coligny), who is now the leader on the
other side, so that your Majesty may be as well informed of what is done there as of what is done here. Of what is
done on that side ⟨we learn nothing except what they are pleased to spread abroad here.⟩ He should be someone who has
some familiarity, acquaintance and credit with them; ⟨and⟩ I think Mr Middlemore would be a very ⟨suitable and fit
man.⟩ As for help, if your Majesty does not intend to recall me, ⟨I have no doubt I shall manage well enough.⟩

⟨I may be deceived, but by every means and source I can find, they intend⟩ to come to no agreement or settlement with
your Majesty: ⟨they would rather⟩ agree to all the Admiral's demands.

02.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, Paris, 27 Jan 1562/3: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (all 32 passages; checked against Forbes ii 315-18).
02.en:
The rendering of Tankervill lieth still in my stomake, bicawse I wolde not have them have any thing whereupon to
glory; as though Englishmen lackid courage to kepe any thing that is tenable by force or policie. In my miend, I had
rather, both by water and land, we had made the profe of our furst strength and constancy there, as of a tast and
essay, before they cam to Newhaven. I pray yow let me know, what opinion ye have of that attempt whereof I wrote to
the queen's majestie by Francis; I meane, whereof I dowtid more of the possibilitie then the comoditie. In my mynde,
it is not to be easely overslipped at this tyme, considering how things do stand even now.

I have written also of a thing now to the queen's majestie, and in both my lettres, which is so necessary, that,
after my phantasy, yt must not be let pas; that is, to have one on the other side with the admirall:

03.summary: Smith to Cecil, Blois, 7 Mar 1562/3 (Forbes ii 350-351): the Guise's death has brought the French "even into my lap"; musters and captains, have all Normandy again this summer; no hostages or assurances for Calais, no quiet holding of Newhaven; the French confess their weakness and need of English friendship; Smith fears only the meddling of the Queen of Scots.
03.en:
⟨The Duke of Guise's death, and the Queen's bold and courageous dealings in paying the Admiral (Coligny) and making
other preparations, had brought them⟩ right into my lap. ⟨You know now what is to be done: you must have⟩ [?musters]
held and captains appointed, ⟨and everything done that can be done⟩ without cost. Let the Admiral know ⟨that you mean
to send a force after him; and if they will not agree to your wishes, that you will⟩ have all Normandy back this summer.
⟨I wish you would show the courage I show them.⟩ I tell them plainly that I know ⟨what money, munitions and captains⟩
they have, ⟨and what men, and what kind of men⟩ they can raise; ⟨and that⟩ the Queen, ⟨now that the season favours it,
will no longer be trifled with.⟩

As for hostages or securities for Calais to be restored later, ⟨I will not hear of it;⟩ no, nor of holding Newhaven (Le
Havre) quietly so long.

04.summary: Smith to the Queen, Blois, 12 Mar 1562/3 (Forbes ii 356-359): a Spanish packet intercepted at Trent reveals a Spanish-Imperial plan against France; the Admiral holds out on the peace terms and is looked for at court; the Spanish ambassador sounds Smith on Caen, Calais and the forfeit crowns; Condé is won over and will help drive the English out of France; the Emperor will denounce war over Metz, Toul and Verdun.
04.en:
⟨It is whispered here that⟩ the King of Spain's ⟨messenger was robbed on the way⟩ to Italy ⟨and his packet brought to⟩
the French Ambassador at Trent, ⟨who on opening it found in the letters a plan⟩ between the King of Spain and the
Emperor ⟨to invade⟩ France, ⟨and has warned the Queen Mother here of it. This is now spreading, and they suspect here
that⟩ the King of Spain and your Majesty are agreed, ⟨and that he would be content for you to make⟩ war on France ⟨to
recover⟩ Calais, and more besides, ⟨if need be. I see nothing very different myself from my friendly talks⟩ with the
Spanish Ambassador. ⟨However⟩ the French ⟨have agreed among themselves, I can learn nothing certain.⟩

⟨I see that a great hold-up⟩ lies with the Admiral, who, as I understand, ⟨does not like the terms as well⟩ as the Prince
(Condé) does, ⟨and holds out stoutly:

05.summary: Smith to Cecil, Amboise, 13 Apr 1563 (Forbes ii 384-386): Condé, sworn in his authority, is thought a new King of Navarre, won by the papists; to deal with the Admiral or d'Andelot is vain, all must be done with the Queen Mother and the Prince; the Spanish ambassador says Philip will not meddle in a quarrel between England and France over Calais or Newhaven; Smith would take Calais.
05.en:
⟨To speak plainly of the state of things here: no one can promise himself any good from them.⟩ The Prince of Condé,
now appointed and sworn into his full authority, is thought ⟨by many of the gentlemen who did most for him and were
closest to him to have become almost⟩ a new King of Navarre (that is, as unreliable as Antoine of Navarre). ⟨They
think he will soon show himself unkind to God, to us and to himself, won over⟩ by the papists, ⟨either by Balaam's
reward or by Cozbi the Midianite.⟩

⟨You will see from my last letters that sending a special envoy to deal with⟩ the Admiral ⟨or with⟩ Monsieur d'Andelot
⟨is useless, especially since you have Mr Middlemore here, who never leaves⟩ the Prince of Condé. ⟨Everything now has to
be done⟩ with the Queen Mother and the Prince.

06.summary: Smith to the Queen, [Valmont] 27/28 July 1563: the Earl of Warwick does not say whether he can keep Newhaven, for how long, or with how many men (CSP vi 1078 §5).
06.en:
My Lord of Warwick (commanding the English garrison in Newhaven, Le Havre).

Whether he is able to hold it or not, [?nor] for how long, nor how many men he has in it.

07.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, Paris, 25 Jan 1563/4: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (large part; checked against CSP F. 7 no. 103).

08.summary: Smith to Cecil, Valence, 1 Sep 1564: the Scots-French practice against the amity of England and Scotland; the Lord of Murray and the lords favouring religion; Huntly; the bishops and the Pope's council; Lethington, his brother at Bruges, the Bishop of Glasgow and a French pension; the Queen of Scots and Lord Robert; the old Pope; the King of Spain and the Queen of Scots (CSP vii 642 §3).
08.en:
Scotland; […]; Scotland. The amity; England; Scotland.

[The] Lord of Murray (James Stewart, Earl of Moray); such lords and great men; [who] are the great supporters of the
(Protestant) religion there.

To do [?some] great enterprise that way. The Scots […]; of the religion; for [?my] […] Lord of Murray.

[?The Earl of] Huntly died, and his sons were taken.

Bishops here; the Pope's council; are as busy as can be.

The Lord of Lethington (Maitland); is at Bruges; the Bishop of Glasgow; pension; […] Lord of Lethington, from the French
King; from the King of Spain.

The Queen of Scots; to [?marry] Lord Robert (Dudley). England and Scotland. […] to the old Pope. England and Scotland.

[?My] Lord of Murray. Of the Queen of Spain. The King of Spain to the Queen of Scots.

09.summary: Smith to Cecil, Valence, 3 Sep 1564: Ninian Cockburn may come into England with Villeroy (CSP vii 650).

10.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, Avignon, 4 Oct 1564: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (about 50 of 62 passages; checked against CSP F. 7 no. 714). Among them: "they feare that she is enclined to this last offer of Lenox".

11.summary: Smith to Cecil, Marseilles, 13 Nov 1564: never in so great a trouble; a post for Scotland goes by Dieppe or by sea, all by the Cardinal of Lorraine; the matter is hot, chiefly the marriage matter, who shall bear the bell away; his men in England by whom he dare speak (CSP vii 793).
11.en:
Scotland. In as great a trouble (as ever). Marriages. In England and Scotland.

Scotland. I must […] knowledge of it; [?he] goes by [?Dieppe], by [?sea], by the Cardinal of Lorraine (all the Scottish
posts pass through the Cardinal).

The matter is hot; it is chiefly the marriage question (of the Queen of Scots), and who shall [carry] the prize.

By whom (Smith's own men, kept in England) I dare speak.

12.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, Arles, 20 Nov 1564: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (large part; checked against CSP F. 7 no. 806). A marginal gloss spells out "Enos" = Ambassador.
12.en:
This [bearer] Adam Hume, I p[erceive] by Mr Alingtons letter which you sent me, was well rewarded. What he deserved I
can not tell; it was he, at the [?least] he was one of them, which with lies and forged invencions to let the peace at
the making thereof made Sir Nicholas almost or altogether mad. [He] [?lay] all this tyme [with] the Ambassador of
Scotland, [?who] […] suspecteth him to be sent from the Protestants of Scotland. The Ambassador is wholly for the
Papistes, and […] glad to be rid of him.

I […] [?understand] now this by Hume['s] small errand […] at I [?marvel]. [?Probably] he had […] [?warned] […]
[?procured] […] of him.

13.summary: Smith to Cecil, Arles, 22 Nov 1564: the Emperor's house (the Archduke Charles) and a marriage with the Queen's Majesty (CSP vii 808).
13.en: The Emperor (that is, the Emperor's house: the Archduke Charles). Marriage with [?there] the Queen (Elizabeth).

14.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, Arles, 24 Nov 1564: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (all but a few signs; checked against CSP F. 7 no. 815). The Cardinal of Lorraine and the Prince of Condé banqueting together at Soissons and Nanteuil, the Guise complaint that the Cardinal's letters are opened at Paris and Lyons, and the bearer Hume "altogether a Lidington ... having pencions of all three princes".
14.en:
The Cardinal of Lorraine and the Prince of Condé have had conferens and familiar banketting togither at Soissons and
at Nanteuil le chasteau, which was the late [?Cardinal] of Burbons, and all to […] […]. This is much noted here.

They of Guise do complaine that all letters that come from the Cardinal, and the […], be [?opened] and […],
principally at Paris and Lyons. This at this […]; and the Embassatour of Scotland and the Cardinal and Madame de Guise
be daily in great dispeches to and from Scotland and to and from the Cardinal of Lorraine, and all by […].

This bearer Hume is altogether a Lidington, whom you shall find double, I am afraid, or rather triple, having […] and
pencions of all three princes.

15.summary: Smith to Cecil, Narbonne, 7 Jan 1564/5: posts out of Scotland, Mr Beton and Hume by land, by the Cardinal of Lorraine, by sea; the house of Guise earnest in the marriage between the Duke of Guise and the Queen of Scots (CSP vii 916).

16.summary: Smith to Cecil, Toulouse, 9 Feb 1564/5: congratulation and condolence; the French and the interview; the Queen's Majesty; the Emperor's house (Charles of Austria); this French offer (CSP vii 979).
16.en:
in the […] congratulation and condolence (the occasions offered and lost).

Of the French; of (the proposed) interview; the Queen; the Emperor (his house: Charles of Austria); [the] French; the
Queen; the Queen; (this) French one (offer).

17.summary: Smith to Cecil, Bourbon-l'Archambault, 22 Mar 1565/6: not that crown; the young King and Queen of Scots; intelligence and practices in England and foreign realms; the Pope's and King of Spain's hands; privy dispatches and couriers out of Scotland; the ambassadors of Spain and Scotland and the Cardinal of Lorraine; the Bishop of Glasgow looks to be a cardinal; popery in Scotland and England; a fat Scottish woman, married, the conveyer of letters to Lady Lennox (CSP viii 208).
17.en:
[?Not] that crown (the Scottish one; they look for a bigger). (That) young [?King] and Queen (Darnley and Mary). Intelligence
and practices in England. Foreign realms.

The Pope's and the King of Spain's [?hands] are in that (dish). French; French; that.

That had both one dispatch. Have seen. Carried, and one […] brought the. A […] secret dispatch of. Nor. From Scotland.
[?Go] unsearched.

The Ambassadors of Spain and Scotland and the Cardinal of Lorraine (consult together) overmuch; the Bishop of Glasgow
expects to be made a cardinal; popery; (not only in) Scotland but also (in) England.

Which (letters) long [?came] out of Scotland. A fat Scottish woman; she was married (to a captain); she is the carrier of
(letters) out of Scotland to the […] (Lady) Lennox. From her; the Queen's […]; her to; be discovered, and […] practices.

18.summary: Smith to Cecil, Paris, 29 Apr 1566: Sturm's letter by Peter Clare, Almain; Albert de Rosemberg; a continuation with the princes of Almain for the recovery of Metz and Calais (CSP viii 327).
18.en:
This letter (from Johann Sturm). Peter Clare. German, and also […]. Albert von Rosenberg.

A continued alliance with the German princes for the recovery of Metz and Calais.

19.summary: Smith to Cecil, Paris, 15 Oct 1562 (Forbes ii 119): Scots report envoys sent to move the Queen of Scots to break with England and make war, and a plan to convey the hostages into Flanders; Secretary Rollet and Monsieur Villemort are gone.
19.en:
⟨You see what Sir Nicholas (Throckmorton) thinks of their Ambassador in England; and I am reliably told by several⟩
Scots ⟨that several men have already been sent, and more will be, to urge⟩ the Queen of Scots to break with you and to
make war ⟨at once; and that it is now in hand and being negotiated⟩ that the hostages you hold shall be conveyed ⟨away
to⟩ Flanders. ⟨For the first matter there have been appointed, and are going or gone,⟩ Secretary Rollet and Monsieur
Villemort.

20.summary: Smith to Cecil, Poissy, 20 Oct 1562 (Forbes ii 123): Newhaven is not so strong as men take it; in summer they would try to drive the English out with "a garden of chamillion upon the hill on this side"; the French works there are not finished.
20.en:
Newhaven (Le Havre) ⟨is not as strong as people think; if it were summer, they would try to drive our men out of it
with a⟩ "garden of chamillion" (Smith's veiled phrase, meaning not settled) on the hill on this side. ⟨Those who know the place will understand
what I mean. And the works begun there by⟩ the French ⟨are not finished.⟩

21.summary: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil, 15/17 Dec 1562: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (all 6 passages; checked against Forbes ii 238). "to trust no Frenchman of what religion soever he be".

22.summary: Smith to the Queen, 4 Nov 1563: De Montaigne, whose carte of La Rochelle Smith sends; letters given him to Lord Robert and Mr Secretary; the other letters he carried himself; the feat Smith wrote of is most necessary at this time (CSP vi 1366).
22.en:
De Montaigne, of whom I [?do] speak, whose map of La Rochelle I have [?sent] herewith; and under another pretext I have
given him letters to my Lord Robert (Dudley) and Mr Secretary (Cecil), to whom I wrote from Rouen about the same
matter. The other letters he carried himself; and in the undertaking I wrote of, I think he can succeed; but this, at
this time, is most necessary.

23.summary: Sir Thomas Smith advertisements from France, 31 Jan 1562/3: the ciphered passages as Patrick Forbes copied them into his deciphering file (Add MS 4136), deciphered with Smith's key R9261 (passage (2) on the queen of Navarre; the rest fragments; checked against not found in Forbes or CSP F. 6).

snip.cap: Add MS 4136 f. 166: Forbes’s copy of Smith’s letter from Arles, 24 November 1564, the Cardinal of Lorraine and Condé conferring at Soissons

system: Homophonic alphabet of symbols (a-m) and digits 2-10 marked bare/dot/colon (n-p, r-s, t-u-y), dotted-letter word codes, about 30 name symbols and a list of null words (English ports, 'and', 'bycause').
